title: Beads That Fold Into Machines
principle: A string of these beads is a protein.

t: Twenty kinds of bead. Join them in any order and the string folds itself into a machine.
Twenty amino acids, joined in any order you like. The chain then folds itself into a specific machine, and the order is the only thing that decided which one.
sub: The same twenty, in everything alive.
Same twenty everywhere, which is why a human gene works in a bacterium.

question: If you swapped two beads over, what would happen?
Exchange two residues in a chain. What is the consequence?
options: It might fold into a completely different shape
It would fold the same but be slightly heavier
stages.outcome: It might fold into a completely different shape
note: Commit. Sickle-cell disease is one amino acid out of 146, which is a fact worth holding while you answer.

t: Fold this string and see what it turns into.
Fold the chain to its best arrangement, then look at the shape you ended up with.
goal: A shape, from nothing but the order of the beads.
A specific structure, produced by sequence alone. No template, no mould, nothing supervising it.

t: A string of these beads is a protein. The beads are amino acids.
A chain of amino acids is a protein, and it is the most versatile of the four families by a long way.
Amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Twenty side chains — oily, watery, acidic, basic, large, tiny — which is the variety that makes the fold specific.

The nucleic acids store and the carbohydrates fuel and the lipids partition, but essentially every action in a cell is taken by a protein. That division of labour is close to universal, and the RNA world hypothesis exists partly because it is hard to see how it could have started that way.
sub: Change one bead and the machine can stop working.
One substitution can abolish the fold entirely, because the shape depends on the whole sequence at once.
Sickle-cell disease is a single glutamate replaced by a valine — one residue in 146 — which puts an oily patch on the outside where there should be a watery one.

That exposed hydrophobic patch makes deoxygenated haemoglobin polymerise into fibres, which deform the cell. One residue, one exposed surface, and a disease — and the same allele confers malaria resistance in carriers, which is why selection has not removed it.

q: Why does changing one bead matter so much?
Why can a single substitution abolish function?
Why is the sequence-structure map so unforgiving at some positions and not others?
options: Because the shape depends on the whole order at once
Because one bead is much bigger than the others
Because there are only twenty to choose from
why: The shape comes from all the beads together. Move one and the folding can come out completely different — or leave a sticky bit on the outside where there should not be one.

The fold is a global property of the sequence, so a local change can have a non-local effect. A substitution buried in the core, or one that exposes an oily surface, can wreck the structure; the same change elsewhere may do nothing at all.

Positional sensitivity varies enormously and predictably: buried core residues and active-site residues are highly constrained, surface loops are largely tolerant. This is why conservation across species is such a good predictor of which mutations will be pathogenic — evolution has already run the experiment.

t: This is where the next world starts: the instructions that say what order the beads go in.
The genome does one job — it specifies the order of the beads. Everything in this module follows from that, and the next world is about how those instructions are written, copied and read.
